before: A class defines fields and methods; new Counter() creates an instance. Each instance has its own non-static value field. A method call through a reference operates on that referenced object.
Counter b = new Counter() creates a second object. Counter b = a instead copies the reference: both variables then refer to the same object. It does not clone the fields.

The package-private Counter can share this Main.java file; only Main is public. With no written constructor, this class gets a default no-argument constructor. value starts at the explicitly supplied 0.

Expected output or behavior: 0 1
. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
Optional local transfer task: Create three counters, alias two references, and trace which fields a method changes. You may trace it without a JDK; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: A class describes data fields and methods for objects. An instance is one object made from that class. Each Counter here has its own value field. Calling increment changes the counter reached through that reference.
Each new Counter() makes a separate object. Assigning a to b instead copies a reference, so both names point to one object. It does not make another Counter.

Main is the public class in Main.java. Counter has no public keyword and can share the file. Since Counter declares no constructor, Java supplies a no-input constructor to create it. Its value field is set to zero.
The program prints 0 1. Only b's counter is incremented, so a's counter stays at zero.
The quiz makes b point to a's object. Decide which count both names will read after b.increment().
